questions.q: What is the key difference between equal weighting and signal weighting?
options: Equal weighting uses leverage; signal weighting never does
Equal weighting splits capital evenly across selected names regardless of signal strength; signal weighting scales each position by the strength of its own signal value
Signal weighting can only be used for currencies
There is no practical difference between the two
questions.explain: Equal weighting treats all selected names the same once they clear the selection bar, while signal weighting gives more capital to names the signal is more convicted about.

questions.q: What does inverse-volatility weighting attempt to equalize across positions?
options: The dollar amount invested in each position
The number of shares held in each position
Each position's contribution to overall portfolio risk, not its dollar allocation
The signal strength of each position
questions.explain: Inverse-volatility weighting sizes a low-volatility asset with a larger dollar position than a high-volatility one, so each ends up contributing roughly equal risk to the portfolio rather than equal capital.

questions.q: Why is mean-variance (Markowitz) optimization described as fragile in practice, despite being mathematically optimal?
options: It cannot be computed for more than two assets
It is extremely sensitive to small estimation errors in expected returns, which can produce extreme, unstable, concentrated weights
It requires real-time data feeds that don't exist
It ignores volatility entirely
questions.explain: Mean-variance optimization uses the full covariance matrix and an expected return vector; because expected returns are hard to estimate precisely, small errors in that estimate can swing the optimizer toward extreme, unreliable weights.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do simpler construction methods (equal weight, inverse volatility) sometimes outperform mean-variance optimization out-of-sample?
options: Because simpler methods always have lower transaction costs
Because mean-variance optimization's sensitivity to noisy expected-return estimates often produces worse real-world results than its theoretical optimality suggests
Because mean-variance optimization is illegal in most markets
Because simpler methods require more historical data
questions.explain: The lesson explains that because the inputs (expected returns) to mean-variance optimization are unreliable, the resulting 'optimal' weights can perform worse out-of-sample than much simpler, more robust construction methods.

questions.q: What does a "long-short, market-neutral" portfolio construction aim to achieve?
options: Maximum leverage on the most attractive names
Long attractive names and short unattractive ones, designed so returns depend on relative performance rather than overall market direction
Holding only cash positions
Avoiding all short positions
questions.explain: Long-short, market-neutral construction pairs long and short positions so that net market exposure (and sometimes net beta) is close to zero, aiming for the strategy's P&L to depend on the signal's relative calls rather than the market's overall direction.
